summary: A 1975 official change to the Host-Host Protocol that clears up an ambiguity about the ERR command. It changes the documents NIC 8246 and NIC 7104.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 695 corrects an ambiguity in the Host-to-Host Protocol's ERR command. It gives separate error codes to a request on a non-open socket, a message on an unknown link, and an invalid host header.

questions: what does host-host error code 5 mean
subtitle: A protocol correction that assigns separate ERR codes to distinct error cases.

tldr.problem: Host-Host Protocol error code 5 covered two cases whose ERR data fields had different formats, so a receiver could not reliably tell them apart.
tldr.mechanism: The correction defines code 5 for a request on a non-open socket, code 6 for a message on an unknown link, and code 7 for an invalid host header.
tldr.outcome: An NCP can use the error code to distinguish the three cases and interpret the accompanying data field.

today: RFC 695 is an official change to the Host-to-Host Protocol, issued in July 1975. It corrects the ERR command definition in the protocol document.

sections.title: Why Error Code 5 Was Ambiguous
sections.content:
The earlier protocol used ERR code 5 for both a control command referring to a socket that was not fully open or closed and a non-control message arriving on a link not used for a connection.

The data field held a command in the first case and a message header in the second. A receiving NCP or a person reading an error log could not reliably distinguish them.
sections.plainLanguage: One error number described two different problems. Their data had different formats, but the number alone did not show which problem occurred.

sections.title: The New Error-Code Meanings
sections.content:
The replacement text assigns error code 5 to a request other than STR or RTS on a socket that is not part of a fully established connection. Code 6 means a message arrived over a user link not currently used by a connection.

Code 7 means a message on the control link or a valid user link had an invalid host header. The RFC gives examples such as invalid M1 or M2 fields, invalid byte size, or a declared length greater than the actual length.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the three error codes now identifies one case. The receiver can interpret the accompanying command or message header using the code.

sections.title: Effect of the Change
sections.content:
The memo replaces paragraph f under “ERR - Error detected” in the Host-Host Protocol. The data field for each new code is defined for its corresponding case, including any zero fill described in the replacement text.

This is an official change to be filed with the protocol specification and the Current Network Protocols Notebook.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo replaces the ambiguous paragraph in the protocol documentation. It makes the ERR command's data easier to interpret.
